title: From 30-60-90 to 3-6-9: organized disruption in practice
summary: Unisys CEO Mike Thomson explains why the 30-60-90 day planning cycle no longer fits the pace of AI adoption, and how organized disruption gives leaders a practical framework for moving fast without breaking what matters.
body_text: Where will we be in three days? That was the question I put to my team when they presented a detailed 30-60-90 day training rollout. The team had not been thinking in those terms. And that gap, between the planning cadence we default to and the pace at which this technology is moving, is where most organizations are steadily losing ground. The 30-60-90-day plan is not wrong. It served us well for a long time. But it was built for conditions that no longer apply. When the model your team trained six months ago has already been superseded, when new tools arrive faster than procurement cycles can process them, and when your competitors measure progress in weeks rather than quarters, the planning rhythm itself becomes the bottleneck. The only way through is to form a fundamentally different relationship with disruption. Rethinking disruption Most organizations treat disruption as something to be managed, minimized, or explained away. When a new technology initiative causes friction, the instinct is to slow down, smooth things over, and restore a sense of stability. That instinct is understandable. It is also expensive. Every significant technology shift over the past 50 years has come through disruptors, organizations and leaders willing to move at a pace that felt uncomfortable. Those who held back and waited for certainty didn’t find safety. They found irrelevance. Think about what happened to the companies that treated the shift to cloud , to mobile, to digital commerce as something to observe before committing. The window closed on them. They spent years trying to catch up to competitors who had already moved on. What we are experiencing now is the same dynamic at a faster speed. Analysts, advisors, and the organizations we work with every day are consistent on this point: AI represents the most significant disruptive shift in technology history. If your organization does not feel some level of productive discomfort right now, that is worth examining. What organized disruption means for AI adoption There is a meaningful difference between disruption as chaos and disruption as strategy. Organized disruption is not disruption for its own sake. It is a deliberate, sequenced approach to layering in AI that proves the technology in controlled ways before it becomes standard practice, moving at pace without breaking the operational continuity your clients and your business depend on. Every organization carries technical debt , a backlog of aging systems, tools, and infrastructure built for a previous era, each with a natural point at which it needs to be replaced or modernized . Some systems in your environment are due for a refresh in the next few months. Others in years. Rather than treating AI adoption as a separate initiative running alongside your existing roadmap, align it to that refresh cycle. As each system approaches its replacement point, ask what it should look like with AI capabilities built in. Over time, what felt disruptive at the start becomes your new standard operating model. This is what it means to treat AI as a process rather than an event. Organizations that approach it as a one-time deployment, a project with a start date and an end date, consistently underperform those that build and refine that capability over time. The pace stays high. The risk stays manageable. And the disruption compounds in your favor. Shifting your internal clock Returning to where we started, the 30-60-90-day plan reflects how an organization approaches time, urgency, and decision-making. Shifting that internal clock runs deeper than updating a template. Approval processes, commitment thresholds, and the expectation of a comprehensive business case before anything moves, all of these were designed for a slower pace and carry a cost that rarely shows up on a balance sheet. Every month spent in planning mode is a month your team is not building the capability that will matter in 2027. There is a practical test I apply to any AI initiative: if we waited six months to get this “perfect,” what would we have missed? The first-mover advantage in AI is about building organizational fluency: the accumulated learning, refined processes, and growing pool of people who know how to make these tools work in your specific environment, which competitors cannot replicate quickly. We saw this directly when our team produced a 91-page RFI response for a prospective client in one week. The same work had previously taken two months. The difference was not the AI tool. It was the accumulated organizational capability: the content library, the documented service frameworks and the team's fluency with AI-assisted drafting, built over time. We could not have moved at that pace if we had waited to start. What this requires of leaders Organized disruption requires leaders who are willing to set a faster cadence, protect space for experimentation and resist organizational pressure to wait for complete certainty before moving. The other requirement is honest self-assessment. Knowing how your systems behave across compliance requirements, data structures , and the specific constraints of your industry determines whether a deployment compounds over time or creates unanticipated problems. Three questions worth asking your leadership team right now: Where can we begin layering in AI capabilities in the next 30 days — not planning for it, but starting? Which approval or planning processes are slowing our decision-making in ways that no longer serve us? Do we have the infrastructure knowledge to deploy AI in a way that improves operations without disrupting what our clients depend on? The answers will tell you where to start. Ready to build your AI adoption roadmap? Contact us to learn how Unisys helps organizations sequence AI investments and build the organizational capability to make them work.

title: How Long Does AncestryDNA Take?
summary: AncestryDNA is one of the most well-known genetic genealogy providers available, but how long does it take for AncestryDNA to deliver?
body_text: You have finally decided to take your DNA test to link yourself to your genetic family tree. You are just about to order your DNA kit from Ancestry . Now comes the hard part, the waiting period. DNA testing takes a series of long processes - from requesting a kit, gathering your saliva sample, to actually sending back your DNA results. AncestryDNA is one of the most well-known genetic genealogy providers available, but how long does it take for AncestryDNA to deliver results? How Much Time Does AncestryDNA Take According to AncestryDNA , your results should be ready in 6 to 8 weeks, starting from the day you receive your DNA test kit from the lab. Before sending in your DNA sample, you must first go to the Ancestry website to create an account if you don’t have one and then activate your DNA test, which will link your sample to your Ancestry account. Your saliva sample will be taken to a secure 3rd party laboratory in the United States to carry out the test. While you wait for results, there are a couple of valuable features provided by Ancestry that you can play with, like the family tree builder. If you don’t activate your DNA kit, Ancestry won’t know who the sample belongs to, and they won’t start processing your sample until you activate the kits. However, you will need to be a member to get full access to their database. Why Does It Take So Long to Process Ancestry DNA? There are several steps involved in the process when it comes to DNA testing, and each one takes time to complete. For instance, you have to wait to receive the kit, take your spit sample, return the kit, wait for the lab to decode your DNA, and get your results. When you order your DNA kit from AncestryDNA, you can either choose standard or expedited shipping. With standard shipping, you can receive your kit in about two weeks, while expedited shipping should get to you in just about three days. Once you seal up your DNA kit and send it, you will have to wait for the lab to receive and process it. The test goes through these stages: The processing lab receives your kit Your DNA sample is positioned for processing Your DNA is extracted from the sample you provided Your DNA is analyzed and entered into the database Your DNA results are displayed These stages take about 14 days, and you can track them through your AncestryDNA account. How Does the Ancestry DNA Kit Work? Once you order the DNA kit from Ancestry, it’ll arrive in the post within a couple of days. Inside the kit, you’ll find the DNA collection tube for a saliva sample, instruction booklet, stabilizing fluid, prepaid return package, and collection bag. You are required to spit into the tube until it reaches the designated line. However, keep in mind that it takes more effort to fill the tube than you might think, so you shouldn’t drink or eat for about an hour before spitting into the tube. Then, send your saliva sample back to AncestryDNA in the envelope provided. Can You Use AncestryDNA for Genealogy? AncestryDNA is valuable for genealogy and building your family tree. It can help guide your research and give you the information you need to build your family tree. The people on your DNA match lists are related to you somehow, and many of them also have family trees ascribed to their DNA results. You can study the family trees of your DNA matches to identify your common ancestor. You can use your AncestryDNA results to discover new collateral lines in your family. More advanced DNA match analysis tactics can help you recognize and figure out how you are related to your DNA matches. Leeds Method and Chromosome mapping are the two such strategies suitable for beginners who want to take their DNA results to a new level. What Can You Do If Your DNA Results Is Taking Too Long? If your Ancestry DNA result is taking too long, here are some things to check if your DNA result takes more than eight weeks to process: Check Your Spam Folder: The company usually sends applicant emails at each stage of the process. If you do not get this notification, the first step is to check your promotions or spam folder to check if the emails are there. It is possible that you missed an email that informs you that your DNA sample process has failed. Make Sure You Activate Your Ancestry Kit: If you have not received any email from Ancestry after a few weeks of sending your sample, you may have forgotten to activate your DNA kit. Else, the lab will hold on to a DNA sample that they can’t connect to any particular account. Lost DNA Kit: If you mailed your DNA kit and have already activated your DNA kit and still, Ancestry hasn’t received it after several weeks, it may have got lost in transit. title: Apollo vs. Outreach: Which should you choose in 2026?
summary: An honest 2026 comparison of Apollo and Outreach across data, sequencing, governance, AI, and pricing, with clear guidance on who each one fits.
body_text: Apollo and Outreach both run sales sequences, but they answer different problems. Apollo is an affordable all-in-one that bundles a large contact database with sequencing and light dialing, best for teams that are assembling their first stack. Outreach is an enterprise sequencing platform with deep workflow governance, best for large sales orgs that already own their data. The two invite comparison because their sequencing features overlap. Underneath this, they sit in different categories. Apollo starts from data and adds cadence on top. Outreach starts from cadence governance and expects you to bring data. Which one is right turns on where your team is in its growth, how disciplined your process needs to be, and whether you want to buy leads and outreach in one place. Here is the honest comparison. How Apollo and Outreach compare Apollo Outreach Best for Teams that want data and cadence in one affordable tool Large, disciplined sales orgs that need workflow governance Native database Yes, over 230M contacts claimed No, you bring your own data Standout capability Bundled database plus sequencing and light dialing Mature sequence controls, permissions, reporting AI layer Assistive AI, plus Pocus signals (acquired Mar 2026) Omni agent (added Apr 2026) Public pricing Free to about $119/user/month, per its pricing page ~$100 to $165/user/month reported Model Per-seat, self-serve Per-seat, enterprise sales-led What is the core difference between Apollo and Outreach? Apollo is a data-first all-in-one. Its center of gravity is the contact database, and the sequencer, light dialing, and enrichment are built around moving those contacts into outreach cheaply. This is why smaller teams reach for it as a first stack: leads and cadence in one bill, often starting free. Outreach is a cadence-first enterprise platform. It assumes you already have a data source and a defined sales process, and it exists to run this process at scale with control. Sequence management, team permissions, step-level analytics, and reporting are the product. Many enterprises run Outreach on top of a separate data provider precisely because Outreach is the execution and governance layer, not the data layer. Which has better data and prospecting? Apollo, clearly, because a native database is its whole premise. It claims over 230M contacts and is used by more than 600,000 companies per its own figures, and its March 2026 acquisition of Pocus added signal-based selling to the prospecting side. For a team that wants to search for leads, enrich them, and drop them into a sequence in one tool, Apollo does this at a price point Outreach does not try to match. For related comparisons, see Apollo vs. Lusha and Clay vs. Apollo . Outreach does not ship a prospecting database. It is designed to sequence contacts you supply from a CRM or a data vendor. This is not a weakness in its category; it is a deliberate scope. But if part of what you are shopping for is where the leads come from, Apollo answers this question and Outreach does not. For how Apollo stacks up against other data providers, see ZoomInfo vs. Apollo and Seamless vs. Apollo . Which is better for enterprise sequencing and governance? Outreach. Its reputation is built on workflow discipline for large teams: granular sequence controls, role and team permissions, approval structures, and reporting that revenue operations leaders can actually govern. When a sales org has dozens or hundreds of reps and needs consistent process enforcement, Outreach is the more mature answer, and reported pricing around $100 to $165/user/month reflects that positioning. Apollo can run sequences at scale too, and plenty of mid-market teams do. The difference shows up in governance depth and how enterprises treat the tool. Larger buyers often use Apollo as a data layer that feeds a more controlled execution platform, rather than as the system of record for a disciplined outbound process. If tight process control across a big team is the priority, Outreach earns its premium. What about AI features? Both added AI, and both kept a human in the driver's seat. Apollo's AI is assistive: it helps write and research, and Pocus brings signal-based selling into the prospecting flow after the March 2026 acquisition. Outreach introduced its Omni agent in April 2026 to pull more AI into sequencing and rep workflows. The shared limit is the model. In both tools a rep still owns the motion. The AI drafts and suggests, but a person decides, sends, and follows up. Neither is trying to run the outbound job on its own, which matters if what you actually want is fewer manual steps rather than better manual steps. How do Apollo and Outreach compare on price? Apollo is the cheaper entry by a wide margin. It runs from free to about $119/user/month per its pricing page, which is why first-stack teams gravitate to it. This number covers data, sequencing, and light dialing. Outreach is an enterprise purchase. Reported pricing sits around $100 to $165/user/month, sold through a sales process rather than self-serve, and this does not include the separate data source most Outreach customers run alongside it. So the real stack cost for an Outreach shop is the seat price plus a data vendor, where Apollo folds both into one lower bill. Price alone favors Apollo; governance and scale are what justify Outreach. A third option to know about The shared limitation is easy to overlook when you are weighing data against governance: in both Apollo and Outreach the AI is assistive, not autonomous, and a human rep still runs the motion. You are choosing which sequencer to drive, not whether to drive one. If neither a data-first bundle nor a rep-governance platform is really what you want, and the goal is to have the outbound work done rather than orchestrated, an autonomous platform is a third path. Artisan built Ava, an autonomous AI business development representative (BDR) , to source, write, send, reply, and book meetings on her own, with a built-in dialer for the calls your reps make, on usage-based pricing sized to lead volume rather than a seat per rep. For a direct comparison, see Artisan vs. Apollo . It is a different category from either tool here: the AI runs the sequence instead of a rep operating it. Choose Apollo if... You are assembling your first stack and want leads and cadence in one affordable tool. You want a native contact database rather than paying a separate data vendor. Your team is small to mid-market and price sensitivity matters more than deep governance. You want to start free or self-serve and grow into paid tiers. Signal-based prospecting through Pocus fits how you want to find accounts. Choose Outreach if... You run a large, disciplined sales org that needs strict sequence and permission controls. You already have a data source and want a dedicated execution and governance layer. Reporting and process consistency across many reps is a top requirement. You are comfortable with an enterprise, sales-led purchase and per-seat pricing. You want the Omni agent inside a mature, well-governed sequencing platform. Frequently asked questions Is Apollo or Outreach better for a small team? Apollo, in most cases. It bundles a contact database with sequencing and light dialing from free to about $119/user/month, so a small team covers leads and cadence in one affordable tool without buying a separate data vendor. Outreach is built for large, disciplined orgs and priced accordingly at a reported $100 to $165/user/month, with data supplied separately, which is usually more platform than a small team needs. Does Outreach include a contact database like Apollo? No. Outreach is a cadence and governance platform that expects you to bring contacts from a CRM or a data provider. Apollo's whole premise is the native database, claimed at over 230M contacts. If having leads inside the same tool matters to you, this is a real point for Apollo; if you already have a strong data source, Outreach's execution layer is the reason to choose it. For a data-provider matchup, see Apollo vs. ZoomInfo . Which has better AI, Apollo or Outreach? Both added assistive AI in 2026 and both keep a human running the motion. Apollo's AI helps write and research, and its March 2026 Pocus acquisition added signal-based selling. Outreach introduced its Omni agent in April 2026 for sequencing and rep workflows. Neither runs outbound autonomously; the rep still decides and sends. If autonomous execution is the goal, both fall short of it by design. How much do Apollo and Outreach cost? Apollo runs from free to about $119/user/month per its pricing page. Outreach does not publish self-serve pricing; reported figures put it around $100 to $165/user/month through an enterprise sales process, and most Outreach customers pay for a separate data vendor on top. So Apollo is meaningfully cheaper once you account for the full stack. Is there an alternative to both Apollo and Outreach? Yes. Both keep a human rep running the sequence; if you want the outbound job done rather than orchestrated, an autonomous platform is the alternative. Artisan's AI BDR, Ava, sources, writes, sends, replies, and books meetings on her own, with a dialer your reps use for calls, on usage-based pricing sized to lead volume instead of per-seat fees, so the AI runs the motion rather than assisting a rep who does. See Artisan's AI sales agent for how that model differs from a data-first bundle or a governance platform. For other data-first options, see the best Apollo alternatives . Can you use Apollo and Outreach together? Some teams do, using Apollo as a data source that feeds contacts into Outreach for execution and governance. It works, but you are paying for two tools and stitching them together. If this is your setup, weigh whether Apollo's own sequencer already covers your needs, or whether a single platform that includes both data and execution would be cheaper and simpler. You might also weigh other Apollo alternatives . Which is more future-proof given recent moves? Both are actively investing. Apollo added Pocus in March 2026 and reports around $200M in ARR, which points to momentum on the data and signals side. Outreach shipped its Omni agent in April 2026, pushing further into AI-assisted sequencing. Neither shows the roadmap uncertainty that follows a major merger, so the choice comes down to fit rather than stability.

title: Nixxy Announces Strategic AI Infrastructure Platform Initiative
body_text: NEW YORK--( BUSINESS WIRE )--Nixxy, Inc. (Nasdaq: NIXX) today announced it is currently in negotiations directly with the developer of the Nakota project to procure the Nakota property and provide all funds required to obtain the necessary permits and approvals to advance the project. In addition, the company is working on a long-term global definitive agreement to acquire the entire project. The new structure will allow Nixxy to own a much larger percentage of the Nakota project than previously contemplated. Reaffirming Commitment to Nakota Development The Company reaffirmed that it remains committed to advancing the Nakota development opportunity. The evaluation process reinforced Nixxy's confidence in the Nakota opportunity and highlighted the value of a more direct role in advancing its development. Now, Nixxy has greater flexibility to advance Nakota as a cornerstone of its broader AI infrastructure platform and to engage directly with strategic capital, infrastructure, and commercial partners. Therefore, given this strategic initiative, the previously disclosed Letter of Intent relating to the proposed Tachyon9 transaction has concluded upon its expiration. Management and the Board of Directors believe the evaluation process strengthened the Company's strategic direction and supported a broader, more compelling long-term strategy focused on artificial intelligence infrastructure and digital energy development. “Over the past several months, we have continued to evaluate the extraordinary pace of investment occurring across the AI ecosystem. That work reinforced our belief that the greatest long-term opportunity is not simply participating in individual transactions, but building a platform capable of developing, owning, financing, and operating the infrastructure that powers artificial intelligence,” said Chairman and CEO David Kratochvil. Nakota Project Nakota is envisioned as a next-generation AI infrastructure campus integrating dedicated power generation, natural gas infrastructure, digital infrastructure, and scalable expansion capabilities designed to support the rapidly growing demand for artificial intelligence computing. The Company intends to continue advancing development activities while evaluating strategic capital partners, customers, and infrastructure investors to support the project's long-term growth. Looking Ahead The Company believes that artificial intelligence represents one of the largest infrastructure investment cycles in modern history. title: Form your Ohio LLC today
summary: Learn how to register your LLC with the Ohio Secretary of State to start your new business. We’ll walk you through each step and state-specific rules.
body_text: The Buckeye State business advantage: Why start an Ohio LLC? The primary benefit of making your business an LLC is asset protection. If your business incurs debts or faces legal action, your personal assets are generally shielded from any settlements that arise. An LLC is a separate legal entity from its members. It can sign contracts, buy property, and take out loans in its own name. This helps you separate your professional and personal life, both for legal reasons and to increase the credibility of your business. Ohio is a business-friendly state, with favorable laws for small business owners. Here are some of the ways Ohio works to help businesses thrive. No annual reports. Unlike most states, Ohio doesn’t require businesses to file an annual report. In fact, the state has no ongoing state fee for most LLCs , which makes long-term compliance more affordable. No franchise tax. Ohio repealed its franchise tax in 2014. Instead, the state has a commercial activity tax (CAT) with a threshold of $6 million in annual gross receipts, giving small businesses a chance to grow. Tax flexibility. Ohio allows pass-through entities—such as an LLC or S corp —to elect to pay state income taxes at the entity level rather than pass those taxes to the individual owners. This helps owners choose the best tax method for their business. Operational flexibility. Lastly, Ohio only requires LLCs to have at least one member and appoint a statutory agent before filing articles or organization. As long as you maintain compliance, how you operate your LLC is up to you. Before you file: Essential Ohio LLC requirements It’s important to know the requirements for an LLC in Ohio before you start your articles of organization . This helps ensure your forms are error-free and that the Ohio SOS will accept them with no delays. Follow Ohio LLC name rules The Ohio Secretary of State won’t allow you to register a business if its name doesn’t comply with state requirements. Your business name must: Include the words or abbreviations “limited liability company,” “LLC,” “L.L.C.,” “limited,” or “ltd.” You can always file a doing business as (DBA) name if you want to operate under a name without these words, but the formal entity name must include one of them. Be unique—that is, different from existing business names registered with the Ohio SOS and distinguishable enough that it can’t easily be confused. You can conduct a name search on the SOS website to determine if your desired business name is available. Avoid words used to name a government agency (i.e., State Department, CIA, FBI, Treasury, etc.) Stay away from restricted words implying unauthorized association with regulated industries, including words like bank, lawyer, attorney, credit union, or insurance. Terms related to these industries may require additional documentation and proof of licensure paperwork. See Ohio Revised Code Section 1706.07 for a complete listing of the state's naming rules. Identify a statutory agent Ohio law ( Section 1706.09 ) requires you to appoint a statutory agent for your LLC (also called a registered agent in other states). A statutory agent is the person or entity that receives service of process and other formal legal notices on behalf of your LLC. This role is required because it ensures that you can be informed of formal legal notices about your business. A statutory agent can be a person (including yourself or an employee of your LLC) or an entity that offers a statutory agent service. Your agent must: Be resident of Ohio (if an individual) Have a physical address in the state (if an entity) Maintain physical presence on-site during regular business hours Obtain Ohio business licenses and permits Although Ohio doesn’t have a general operating license, LLC owners may need a business license to operate in the state depending on the location and nature of their business. For example, if your LLC sells tangible personal items or taxable services, the LLC must obtain a vendor's license from the Ohio Department of Taxation. This also means you’ll need to collect and pass on sales tax, which ranges from 6.5% to 8% across Ohio.

title: Data Agent Ergonomics
summary: Coding agents are getting good at analysis, but the output is hard to trust and often inefficient. How we think about accuracy and efficiency for data agents.
body_text: Coding agents like Claude Code and Codex are getting good at analysis. They handle the syntax, do the transforms, explain what they find, and anyone on the team can run them without waiting on someone else. The problem is the output is hard for the team to trust. Someone runs an analysis in chat, gets a number, and tries to share it - but the code goes in git, the number goes in Slack, and the reasoning gets lost in between. They ask for a change and the agent starts over. They come back a day later to check the logic and the chat is gone. The answer might be right, but nobody can tell. And they can be inefficient. The agent re-runs pipelines that didn’t change. It drags data through the context window when a pointer would do. It probes schemas one tool call at a time before it can write a single query. The cost adds up, and the budget left for reasoning shrinks. When the work comes back, the team ends up asking two questions: can we trust this (accuracy), and was it worth the cost to get here (efficiency). We think of accuracy as two halves: what the agent does, and what the team can verify. The agent needs to trace its claims back to the data and write transformations the dashboard can re-run. The team needs to follow the reasoning, add data, and redirect when the agent is off. Without both halves, you have an answer nobody can check. Efficiency is about getting to a known answer with the minimum effort and time. Bare agents waste a lot. They re-run pipelines that didn’t change, drag data through the context window, and burn tool calls probing schemas one at a time. Good tooling does most of that work for them, and the savings compound into more budget for reasoning. The next two posts go deeper on each: Accuracy. How we make agent work verifiable and extendable by the team. Efficiency. How a data graph, pointers instead of payloads, and composable typed tools cut agent waste. We’re building BitBoard to solve these problems. We expect to learn a lot about making agents useful along the way. If this interests you, BitBoard’s tool reference, schemas, and example flows are live at docs.bitboard.work .
